# What the attempt-10 amendment settles, and what it leaves untouched

The plan is amended for one file and nothing else. `harness/secrets.py` joins slice 2's
file list and gains a `changes` entry. Everything else in the accepted record stands:
the same four slices, the same points, the same RED per slice, the same rollback, the
same risks, the same answers on migrations, tenant tables, buyer PII and the policy
gate.

**Why the file is in the diff at all.** The review's F4 found the registry carrying no
entry for either of the two checks of the set that have no configuration file, while
`harness/rules.py` said in as many words that both were in the set because both run in
the same pre-commit hook. So the set gained a twenty-third rule,
`harness/no-live-marketplace-host`, and a rule in this registry is provable or it is
padding: every one of the other twenty-two is proven by a fixture its own tool must
refuse. This rule's tool is `secrets.marketplace_hosts`, which walks every tracked file
in any language, and that is precisely why the check is the harness's own rather than an
ast-grep rule, because the same host in a Python fixture or a shell script is the same
defect. A fixture for it is therefore a file in the tree that names a live marketplace
host in a test, and without one line telling the walk to skip `rules/fixtures/`, the
fixture fails the repository's own lint and the rule cannot be proven at all.

**Why that line is in that function and not somewhere else.** Three callers ask the
question: `harness lint`, the triage's deterministic lint check, and `doctor`. Putting
the exclusion in the callers would be one rule written three times, which is the drift
SEEN-097 recorded and the reason `scripts/rules.sh` exists as a single definition. The
walk is the one place the question is answered, so it is where the answer belongs.

**Why it is slice 2 and not a slice of its own.** Slice 2 is the ground rules and the
fixtures that prove them, and it already names `rules/registry.toml`, `rules/fixtures`
and `harness/rules.py`. The twenty-third rule is a ground rule with a fixture, so it is
that slice's work, and the file the fixture needs is that slice's file. A fifth slice
for one line would be a slice plan written for the bookkeeping rather than for the work.

**What is open, and what cannot be.** Nothing in the plan is open. Two things are
decided rather than open and are recorded as decisions, because a gate that cannot tell
a decision from a hole reads the second where the first was meant. gitleaks stays out of
the registry: its fixture would have to carry a string gitleaks detects, which the hook
itself refuses to let anybody commit, so the entry would be a registry line nothing
proves, and the reason is written in `harness/rules.py` where the next person will look.
And `rules/fixtures/` is excluded from one check and from no other control: gitleaks
still scans it on every commit, which is the control that matters for a secret, and what
the exclusion turns off is a check about live hosts in code that no test runner executes.

**What the amendment costs.** Every pair cited by the attempt-9 tdd record was recorded
in that attempt, so the replay runs again here: four slices, the wiring round and the
findings round, then the regression and the coverage last. The rework is a return to
solution and is recorded as one.
